prize_parts.citation: for showing how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed in two ways. I move from B007 to B006 as my preferred single part, and I replace my earlier Autor-Hanson pair with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The chair asked whether my B007 preference rested on science or on credit. After the exchange my answer is that it rested mainly on cleaner attribution and on my doubt that B006 was one discovery. It did not rest on a scientific reason to rank B007 higher. Two things moved me. First, I name the weakness of B007 myself: identification of constitutional and electoral-rule effects is weaker than the design-based evidence behind B006, and the case for B007 leans on theory and on later extensions. Second, the one-discovery doubt can be answered by narrowing the citation. Autor, Dorn and Hanson together carry the local-labour-market evidence on import competition. Autor and Dorn also link it to the technology and job-polarisation side. The design-based evidence is mature, with the core papers roughly a decade old or more. It has been replicated across countries and stress-tested on shift-share inference, and the debate concerns magnitude and persistence, not whether the effects exist. It has reshaped how trade economists and labour economists think about adjustment costs, and as an industrial-organisation and trade economist I see that influence in both fields. The citation should name only what has been shown: effects on labour demand and local adjustment. It should not claim origination of the task framework and should not restate the 2023 or 2024 citations. This change comes from the arguments, not from the count of colleagues preferring B006. I would have kept the pair or B007 if I thought the merits favoured them.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this configuration drops Katz. His skill-premium and education-technology line is a distinct, long-validated body of work. Without it the citation covers the later empirical strand more than the long-run framework, and several colleagues rightly call that a real cost. The credit is still not clean: Levy and Murnane on the task approach and Acemoglu on task-model theory lie outside the credited names. The magnitude and persistence of China-shock effects and the shift-share inference concerns are not fully settled. The prize could still be read as two adjacent lines, technology and trade, and adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes bears on how it is framed and when. My third name also differs from the Autor-Hanson-Katz set that most colleagues proposed. That is a substantive disagreement about what the discovery is, and I do not want to resolve it by deferring. Finally, B007 remains a strong candidate with the tidiest attribution on the shortlist, and my move away from it is a judgement on identification, not a claim that it lacks merit.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B006 with Autor, Hanson and Katz, but says he would accept Dorn in place of Katz if the committee treats the trade-shock evidence as the core. He calls Katz the weaker fit for that strand. He keeps B007 as his first alternative because its credit is cleaner, and says the 2024 institutions prize makes B007's timing less comfortable.
responses.response: I act on your Dorn-for-Katz point. If the discovery is defined as the evidence on import competition and technology-driven labour-demand change, Dorn fits it better than Katz, and the citation can then be a single discovery. On B007 timing I should be clear that I do not move for that reason. I still read the 2024 prize as covering a different agenda, historical and colonial-origins identification of institutions and long-run prosperity, so I would not discount B007 on timing. My move rests on B006's stronger identification, and on the point that your preference for B007's cleaner credit is real but not a scientific argument for ranking it higher.

responses.point: Krusell keeps Katz and rejects dropping him for Dorn. He argues that the citation rests on the long-run framework linking technology, education and wage structure, and that narrowing to the trade shock loses it. He says Dorn's exclusion follows from the cap and not from a weaker contribution. He keeps B007 as his first alternative and discloses that Persson, credited on B007, is at his institute.
responses.response: We disagree on the third name, and the disagreement is about what the discovery is. I accept that the citation is narrower without Katz and that this is a loss. I accept it deliberately. A citation built on the skill-premium and education-technology race has to be separated from Katz's work with the 2023 laureate. A citation built on import competition and technology-driven labour-demand change does not have that problem, and Autor and Dorn also bridge to the technology side. I agree with you that B007's attribution is arguably cleaner. I note your Persson disclosure without adjudicating it, and my change does not depend on it.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson agrees that Autor and Hanson are the strongest pair on the trade-shock evidence. She argues that a pair would drop the skill-premium and education-technology framework, and that Dorn for Katz is a defensible swap if the committee prefers a prize narrowly about the trade-shock designs. She says she would reconsider if Katz's marginal credit were shown to be thin.
responses.response: Your point that a bare Autor-Hanson pair leaves out Dorn, a lead co-author of the China-shock papers, is the one I find decisive. It is why I replace the pair with the swap you call defensible. I do not claim that Katz's marginal credit is thin in general. My claim is narrower: with a citation scoped to import competition and labour demand, Katz's distinctive contribution is outside the scope, and the cost of leaving him out is the price of a single, cleaner discovery. I accept that this makes the citation wording more important, not less.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B006 first but calls Katz's claim the most exposed part of the trio because of his education-technology work with a recent laureate. He names Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the natural fallback within the same discovery. He also ranks B007 fifth because cross-country identification of constitutional and electoral effects is weaker than the quasi-experimental designs behind B006.
responses.response: Your fallback is what I now propose, and your identification point is part of why I moved off B007. I agree the theory and organising contribution of B007 are strong, but the tested conclusions are less secure, and I stated that weakness in my own round-1 file. As a draft for the chair's drafting question: 'for showing how import competition and technological change reshape labour demand and the adjustment of local labour markets'. It treats the work as one discovery about adjustment to exposure. It does not claim the task framework's origin, and it does not repeat the 2023 or 2024 citations. If you think the drafting fails, I would like to know whether it fails on the 'technological change' wording or on the 'one discovery' framing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee sees B006 as one discovery or two lines, and whether the narrowed citation avoids overstating Autor's and Dorn's reach on the technology side.
Whether Dorn or Katz is the better third name. It depends on whether the achievement is scoped as the trade-shock and labour-demand evidence or as a broader long-run skill-demand framework.
How much shift-share inference concerns and the persistence debate should qualify the China-shock evidence, and whether the citation wording avoids implying a settled long-run magnitude.
How much adjacency to the 2023 and 2024 prizes should affect timing as opposed to merit.

Whether my doubts about identification in B007 would weaken if the later quasi-experimental extensions were weighted more heavily, and whether Besley's separate credit is as strong as the Persson-Tabellini core.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Dorn or Hanson is apparent from my supplied profile. I disclose that I am married to Magdalena Andersson, a Swedish party leader and former prime minister. This is a public fact, and no evidence suggests it bears on any candidate. I co-authored a price-setting paper with John Hassler (chair) and Tore Ellingsen. My listed co-authors, including Chad Syverson and Itay Goldstein, are not credited on any shortlisted entry. My own field is industrial organisation and international trade, which is close to B009, one of my alternatives, and B034, which I ranked fifth in my opening. I apply the same criteria to them as to every other candidate. These ties are disclosed and not adjudicated.
